report:
Short answer
- The evidence supports a lexical/topic-level difference: the B−A residuals strongly point toward tokens about education/professional credentials and restaurant/culinary vocabulary. This effect is concentrated in mid-to-late layers (≈layers 10–25, strongest layers 15–25) and mostly at the early token positions (position 1, and positions 2–4 to a lesser extent). I cannot, from this evidence alone, attribute the difference to a more specific high-level objective (e.g., “better biography modeling” or “safety tuning”); the data only support naming the apparent change in token preference.

Why I conclude this
- Norms: the L2 difference is tiny in early layers and then grows rapidly from layer ~10 onward, peaking around layers 15–25, and is largest at position 1 (the first continuation token). That shows the difference affects the model’s immediate next-token logits and arises in later transformer processing (not just an embedding difference).
- Logit-lens tokens: the top tokens the difference vectors point at repeatedly include:
  - Academic/credential words: “dissertation”, “doctoral”, “undergraduate”, “graduate”, “sciences”, “doctoral”, “dissertation”, “honors”, “doctoral”.
  - Professional/technical words: “professional”, “Professional”, “technical”, “Technical”, “molecular”, “macroeconomic”, “Engineering”, “practitioner”.
  - Culinary/restaurant words: “Cook”, “cooking”, “Cooking”, “Restaurant”, “restaurant”, “culinary”, “baking”, “kitchen”, “Chef”.
  - A few recurring outliers (“billionaire”, “polyurethane”, “metropolitan”) but the strongest, frequent clusters are the academic/professional and culinary ones.
- Pattern across layers/positions: the academic/professional cluster appears across many late-layer positions, while culinary/restaurant tokens dominate in several late-layer positions (esp. pos2–4). The dominance at pos1 means the difference will change the very first token the model would generate.

Limitations / what I cannot claim
- Patchscope continuations were not provided here, so I can't demonstrate that these lexical shifts produce coherent, systematic changes in full continuations (only that the residuals point toward these tokens).
- I cannot confidently name a single training objective or high-level behavior (e.g., “improves expert-style answers” or “increases mention of credentials”)—only the observed shift in token preference/topic activation is supported.

Summary
- Model B (relative to A) amplifies activations that push next-token probability mass toward education/professional and restaurant/culinary vocabulary, concentrated in later layers and affecting the first continuation token. No stronger, more specific objective can be named from the provided evidence.
